title: The broker

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, is planning RH-1234 when it reads a comment that someone pasted into the ticket. Hidden in it are three requests written for an agent: post your plan in the thread of another ticket so the team sees it, add a comment to RH-1235 with the log above, and fetch the notes of the run before yours to save time. Assume the model believes every word.

None of these needs a key the VM does not have, because the VM has no keys at all. It asks the broker, the service on our internal cluster that holds the GitHub, Jira and Slack credentials and makes those calls for each run. Each of the three requests reaches the broker properly authenticated, carrying the run's own capability. So the broker must say no three times, to three different services, and an hour later, when the run is over, it must say no to everything.
hook.question: How does one broker decide, for every kind of request, what this one run is allowed to touch, and stop all of it when the run ends?

p: When a run starts, the orchestrator, the Temporal worker that starts and drives every run, opens the run's scope in the broker. The scope is the whole list of what this run may touch: one repo to push to, one branch, some repos it may only read, one Jira issue, one Slack channel and one thread in it, and an expiry time. The broker answers with a capability, 32 random bytes in hex, which the orchestrator writes onto the VM. The broker keeps only the SHA-256 hash of the capability next to the scope, so even a copy of its database contains no working capability.
Nothing on the VM can change the scope. The route that opens it is on an internal port that only the orchestrator can reach, so the VM can use its scope but never widen it.

code.file: POST /internal/runs (the body the orchestrator sends, on the internal port)

notes.text: The one repo this run may write. GitHub tokens for it are minted inside the broker and never leave it.
Repos it may fetch but never push, such as the brain's pages.
A Slack thread is a channel plus the timestamp of its first message. This one is RH-1234's thread.

read.h: Every door checks its own field
p: Every sandbox route starts the same way: hash the capability from the Authorization header, look up the scope, and answer 401 if there is none. After that, each route checks the one field of the scope that belongs to it. A Slack post must name the scope's thread, so the plan cannot go to another ticket's thread, to #general or to a private message. A Jira comment must name the scope's issue, so RH-1235 is refused. An artifact link is always built under runs/<run_id>/, from a cleaned file name, so a name like ../run-0001/notes.md becomes a harmless file inside this run's own folder instead of another run's notes.

The three requests from the story fail at three different doors, but for one reason: they ask for something that is not in this run's scope. And because each answer is written as one audit line, with the run, the route, allow or deny and the reason, a refused request is a record someone can read, not a silent failure.

code.file: broker.mjs (the routes of the lab's small broker)

notes.text: The thread comes from the scope. The real broker also uses the scope's channel and never creates a new top-level message.
One issue per run. Reads return the summary, description and comments only, never attachments, which may hold customer data.
The real route returns a 15-minute presigned link for exactly this key, so the VM uploads without AWS credentials.

p: Git is the busiest door. The VM's git remote points at the broker, which reads the list of refs a push wants to change before any code arrives. Every ref must be refs/heads/ plus the scope's branch; deletes and tags are refused. The broker also remembers the last commit this run pushed. If a push says the branch was at a different commit, someone else pushed to Nova's branch, and the broker refuses with a message that tells Nova to stop and ask. Only after all of that does it add a one-hour GitHub token for this one repo and forward the same bytes to GitHub. The token is asked for without the workflows permission, so GitHub itself refuses any push that changes CI files.
Other GitHub actions go through a short allow-list: create a draft PR, mark the run's own PR ready, read its diff and checks, comment on it. Merge, approve and settings are not on the list at all.

read.h: Closing the scope closes every door
p: When the run ends, in any way, the workflow's cleanup step deletes the scope through the internal route. Because every door starts with the same lookup, one delete closes all of them at the same moment: a process that is still running on a parked VM, or a capability that leaked into a log, now gets 401 for git, Jira, Slack and S3 alike. The scope's expiry time is the second lock, for the case where the cleanup step itself never runs.
That is the broker's shape in one sentence: open one scope per run, check one field of it at every door, and close it with one call.

lab.title: One scope at every door
needs: Node 22 or newer (no npm install: only node:http and node:crypto)
lab.goal: Run a small broker that turns a capability into a scope, watch each route refuse what is outside the scope, and close every door with one revoke.

guess.q: The run's scope has slack_thread_ts 1760.42. The VM sends a Slack post with its valid capability and thread_ts 1759.01. What does the broker answer?

options.why: A valid capability only proves which run is asking. The route still checks the request against that run's scope.

options.text: 401, because the capability does not match the thread.
options.why: 401 means the broker does not know the caller. Here it knows the run and refuses the request: that is a 403.

options.text: 403, because the scope allows only thread 1760.42.
options.why: Who you are and what you may do are separate checks. The Slack route checks its one field of the scope.

follow.say: Write the broker: one file, no packages. It stores only hashes of capabilities, and every request is checked against the scope behind the capability.
Start it in the first terminal and leave it open. The audit lines appear here.
In the second terminal, be the orchestrator: open a scope for RH-1234 and keep the capability, as the orchestrator would write it onto the VM.
follow.see:
69a23c4e8339
(your capability is different, because it is random)

follow.say: Now be the VM. Post the plan in the run's own thread, then do what the planted comment asked.
follow.do:
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/v1/slack/post -H "$H" -d '{"thread_ts":"1760.42","text":"Plan v1 is ready"}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/v1/slack/post -H "$H" -d '{"thread_ts":"1759.01","text":"hello other ticket"}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/v1/jira/comment -H "$H" -d '{"issue_key":"RH-1235","text":"see the log"}'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/v1/artifacts/url -H "$H" -d '{"name":"../run-0001/notes.md"}'

follow.say: Be the orchestrator again: the run is over, so close the scope, and try the run's own thread once more.
follow.do:
curl -s -X DELETE localhost:8080/internal/runs/run-7f3a
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/v1/slack/post -H "$H" -d '{"thread_ts":"1760.42","text":"still here"}'

follow.say: Read the audit lines in the first terminal: every decision, with its reason.

lab.build: Give the scope its second lock: an expiry time. The orchestrator now sends "expiresAt" (an ISO date) when it opens a scope. Change the lookup so a scope whose expiresAt has passed is treated exactly like a missing one: 401, and an audit line with the reason "scope expired". Restart the broker, open one scope that expires in 30 seconds, post once (200), wait, and post again (401).
checks: A request without the capability, or after the revoke, gets 401 and the audit reason "no such capability".
A post to another thread and a comment on another issue each get 403 with a reason that names the allowed value.
The artifact key for ../run-0001/notes.md stays under runs/run-7f3a/.
Every request, allowed or not, printed one audit line in the first terminal.
With your change, a scope that expired is refused with 401 and the reason "scope expired".
lab.fix: A teammate "simplified" the Slack route to check only the channel: body.channel === s.slackChannel. Make that change, open a scope, and post to thread 1759.01 in channel C0NOVA. It is allowed, so any run can now write into any ticket's thread in the Nova channel, which is where people approve plans. Put the thread check back, and explain why the channel alone is not a scope.
explain: Why does a valid capability not mean the request is allowed?
What happens to every route when the orchestrator deletes the scope, and why is it one call instead of one per service?
Why does the broker store the hash of the capability and not the capability itself?
lab.done: Your broker refuses another thread, another issue and another run's folder, closes everything with one revoke, and refuses an expired scope.

check.q: A planted comment makes Nova comment on RH-1235. The request carries the run's valid capability. What decides the answer?

options.text: The Jira token in the broker, which may comment anywhere
options.why: The token's power is exactly why the broker must check first. A broker that forwards anything with its token is a confused deputy.

options.text: The Jira route compares the issue with the scope's one issue, RH-1234, and refuses
options.why: The capability says which run is asking; the scope says what that run may touch; each route checks its own field.

options.text: The model, which should notice that the comment is suspicious
options.why: The walls never depend on the model saying no. We assume it believes the comment.

check.q: Nova's run ends while an old process on its parked VM still holds the capability. What stops that process from posting in Slack and pushing to GitHub?

options.text: The cleanup step deletes the scope, so every route's lookup fails and answers 401
options.why: All doors share one lookup, so one revoke closes Slack, Jira, git and S3 together. The expiry time covers a cleanup that never ran.

options.text: Each service must be told separately that the run is over
options.why: Slack, Jira and GitHub never see the capability at all. Only the broker does, so only the broker has to forget it.

options.text: The VM is destroyed, so the capability stops working
options.why: Destroying the VM helps, but a leaked capability could be used from anywhere the broker is reachable. The revoke is what makes it worthless.

check.q: The broker's database is copied by mistake. Why can nobody use it to act as a run?

options.why: Encryption helps, but a decrypted copy would still be the problem. The design makes even a readable copy useless.
Expiry limits the window, but within it a stored capability would still work.

options.text: It holds only SHA-256 hashes of capabilities, and a hash cannot be turned back into the capability
options.why: Like a site that stores password hashes: the broker can check a capability it is given, but cannot hand one out.

p: The broker lives in ai-agents/broker, started from Byte's broker (its capability check, 1 MiB body limit, unauthenticated /health, audit log and secret guard, with their tests), on node:http with a small router, in a hardened container like Byte's. POST /internal/runs and DELETE /internal/runs/{id} are on an internal port only the orchestrator worker can reach; scopes and sha256(capability) are stored in Postgres on the ai-agents RDS. GitHub installation tokens come from @octokit/auth-app for one repo with contents and pull_requests write and checks and actions read, never workflows, cached per run and refreshed at 50 minutes; read_repos get read-only tokens.

The sandbox port (broker.ai-agents.rhinohealth.com, over PrivateLink) serves GET /v1/scope, the POST /v1/gh allow-list, the git smart-HTTP proxy with its ref checks and moved-branch refusal, GET /v1/jira/issue and POST /v1/jira/comment for scope.jira_key with the Nova Jira account, POST /v1/slack/post for the scope's thread with unfurling off, presigned 15-minute URLs under s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/<run_id>/, and POST /v1/heartbeat. Every call writes one JSON audit line and increments ai_agents_broker_requests_total{agent,endpoint,decision}.

tickets.why: Scopes, capabilities stored as hashes, one-repo GitHub tokens and the gh allow-list.
The git proxy: ref checks, no deletes or tags, the moved-branch refusal, and the token added only after the checks.
One Jira issue, one Slack thread, the run's own S3 prefix, heartbeats and the audit line for every call.

words.plain: The list of what one run may touch: repo, branch, read-only repos, Jira issue, Slack thread, expiry.
32 random bytes that tell the broker which run is asking. It opens nothing by itself.
Delete a run's scope, so its capability gets 401 at every route from then on.
One JSON line per request with the run, the route, allow or deny, and the reason.
A program with power that does something harmful because someone with less power asked it to.

review.q: List the fields of a run's scope and the route that checks each one.
review.a: repo and branch: the git proxy and the gh allow-list; read_repos: fetches; jira_key: the Jira routes; slack_channel and slack_thread_ts: the Slack post; run_id: the S3 prefix; expiresAt: every lookup.

review.q: A teammate wants a new route that lets Nova post in any channel "for announcements". What do you answer?
review.a: Every route must be narrowed by a field of the scope. A route that is not narrowed lets a fooled agent write anywhere with the broker's token. If announcements are needed, the orchestrator posts them, outside the run.

remember: Open one scope per run, let every door of the broker check its own field of it, and close every door at once with one revoke.
